title: [Sponsor] Finalist Daily Planner Meets iPhone Duo
content:
Finalist has always been a paper planner in software, and now iPhone Duo is the perfect iPhone for it. Customize each Duo pose:

  • Closed: agenda with outstanding habits.
  • Opened: timeline on the left and the tasks on the right, drag across to pencil in your day.
  • Propped like a laptop: keep an eye on time left before your next task, with agenda below.

It’s as flexible as your iPhone Duo, with Markdown notes that work in Obsidian, planner swimlanes, Journal, Pencil sketches, Reminders, and Lists.

Apple picked it for Apps that shine on iPhone Duo. And it works great on iPhone, iPad, Mac and Watch.

 ★

title: Finite Projective Spaces
content:
Just as there are finite projective planes, there are also finite projective spaces of higher dimension.

The axioms of a projective space are

  1. Any two distinct points lie on exactly one line.
  2. If A, B, C, and D are distinct points and the lines AB and CD meet, then the lines AC and BD also meet.
  3. Every line contains at least three points.
  4. There are at least two lines.

The second axiom is subtly different from its counterpart for projective planes. It allows for skew lines but not parallel lines. There’s no explicit concept of dimension in these axioms, but dimension can be well-defined by induction.

What I find most interesting about finite projective spaces is that they are in some sense simpler than projective planes. Usually higher dimensions allow for more complicated behavior, but at least as far as classification goes, higher dimensional spaces are simpler.

Finite projective planes are not determined by the number of points they contain. As mentioned in this post, there are four different projective planes with 10 points. It is unknown how many different projective planes there are with 17 points; there are at least 22. But for dimension d ≥ 3, there is at most one projective space with a specified number of points.

Given a prime power q, there is a unique field F with q elements, and one can construct a projective space of dimension d over F analogously to how one constructs a real projective space of dimension d: Take the non-zero vectors in Fd + 1 and mod out by non-zero scalar multiples. And up to isomorphism this is the only way to construct a finite projective space if d ≥ 3. In technical terms, finite projective planes can be non-Desarguesian but higher-dimensionsal projective spaces cannot.

  • Finite affine planes
  • Finite hyperbolic planes
  • Combinatorial designs

title: Am I A Design Engineer?
content:
If you ask me, “What is design engineering?” part of me wants to respond, “I know it when I see it.” In other words: I can’t tell you all that it is, but I can tell you what it is not.

To me, design engineering is not defined by:

  • Making fancy micro-interactions and posting them to Twitter.
  • Making elaborate animations for marketing websites.
  • Constructing elaborate prototypes in a design tool (e.g. Figma) that have no basis in the reality of 1) how browsers work, or 2) your company’s source space.

Despite these personal beliefs about the term, I find its colloquial use different. Here’s my perception of terms these days:

  • “Design Engineer” — too heavily weighted towards visual design and animation, not enough weight in the work of practical engineering.
  • “Product Engineer” — too heavily weighted towards factory engineering (e.g. can you manage agents upon agents within a system to churn out something fast?) and not enough weight in design/product thinking.

Which makes me want to (selfishly) invent another term: Product Design Engineer.

  • Pro: it covers multiple disciplines; Product, Design, and Engineering.
  • Con: it covers multiple disciplines; what a diluted mouthful.

But merely combining nouns doesn’t describe the work. To me, design engineering isn’t about encompassing multiple disciplines. It’s about working in the relationships between them.

For this reason, I’ve always been partial to the idea of Human-Computer Interaction. HCI is fundamentally multidisciplinary, so people with varied interests and backgrounds in computers (design, engineering, product, etc.) and humans (psychology, art, literature, etc.) contribute to its success.

I tend to think of the role of a design engineer to be along the lines of asking questions like:

  • How do computers work? What are they good at? What are they bad at?
  • How do humans work? What are they good at? What are they bad at?

With that framing, you then ask: “Given some human problem, how can I leverage computation (if at all) to solve it?”

Maybe that solution comes in the form of a humane interface, or a better button, or clearer prose, or an optimized API call, or maybe just an email/text.

Or maybe it’s no software at all. Because design engineers live in the relationships between disciplines, I believe they are well positioned to understand a problem and argue that additional software may be a worse, not better, solution.

Maybe I’m not even describing “design engineering” anymore. Maybe I’m just describing the kind of work I enjoy doing and wishing there was a label for it. “Jim Nielsen–Style Software Maker.” If you’re looking to fill that role, I know a guy.

title: Comments and emails
content:
I'm regularly asked why Bear doesn't have built-in comments, guestbooks, or contact forms. They're all trivial to build (a text box and a send button), and I could add them in an afternoon. But they're not included by design.

The problem with all three is what they let in. A comment box or contact form accepts anything from anyone. Spam bots find them quickly, so whoever runs the blog ends up moderating a queue. And the people who comment don't have to identify themselves as most of these forms ask for a name and email address and check neither.

This week a blogger on Bear received a particularly nasty message via an embedded, third-party contact form on their blog, the sender could type anything into the email boxes and press send. It was signed with a fake name, and used the public email address of another blogger, essentially impersonating someone else to stir up trouble. What arrived was, in effect, a shitty, anonymous note.

Anonymous notes are the worst kind to receive. There's nobody to reply to, nothing to block, and the perpetrator doesn't have a social incentive to behave.

This is why Bear's solution to all three is a link with your email address in it (and if you're worried about scrapers, use a dedicated alias or separate address). Your email provider already does the heavy lifting on spam filtering, and a message generally has to come from a real account you can reply to or block. A contact form would have to recreate that verification with confirmation links, and most don't bother.

Naturally, people can still get nasty emails from throwaway accounts, but the sender still has to set up that account or alias first, which adds just enough friction to discourage it. I suspect most nastiness online is impulsive, and the friction of email is just enough to let that impulse pass.

I wrote recently that good systems are ones that well-behaved people barely notice. Email works the same way. A reader who wants to say they enjoyed your post already has an address, and is happy for you to see it. Someone wanting to stay completely anonymous to send a shitty email has to go out of their way to set it up.

If you'd like readers to be able to reach you, the docs explain how to set up a reply via email link and a guestbook that runs on email.

And if you think I'm wrong about any of this, you can get in touch with me here.
